title: Chapter 3: Complex Numbers II: Polynomials & de Moivre

questions.stem: A real-coefficient cubic \(P(z)\) has roots \(3\) and \(2+i\). Which is \(P(z)\)?
questions.hint: A non-real root of a real-coefficient polynomial brings its conjugate with it.

steps.explain: Expand and identify the matching option.

keyPoints.text: A real-coefficient cubic \(P(z)\) has roots \(3\) and \(2+i\)
keyPoints.note: A non-real root of a real-coefficient polynomial brings its conjugate with it.

questions.stem: \(1+2i\) is a root of the equation \(z^3-z^2+qz+5=0\). The value of \(q\) is:
questions.hint: Use the conjugate root, find the third root from the product of roots, then use the sum of pairwise products.

steps.explain: The coefficients are real, so by the conjugate root theorem \(1-2i\) is also a root. Call the third root \(\alpha\).
Product of the roots of \(az^3+bz^2+cz+d=0\) is \(-\frac da\).
Sum of the roots taken two at a time is \(\frac ca=q\).
Check: with \(q=3\), \(z=-1\) gives \(-1-1-3+5=0\) ✓. So \(q=3\), option C.

keyPoints.note: Real coefficients ⇒ 1 − 2i is also a root. Then use product of roots and sum of products in pairs.

questions.stem: Two of the roots of the equation \(z^4+Bz^3+Cz^2+Dz+E=0\), where \(B,C,D,E\) are real are \(3+i\) and \(1-2i\). The value of \(E\) is:
questions.hint: Add the conjugate roots, then use: product of roots of a monic quartic = E.

steps.explain: The coefficients are real, so the conjugates are also roots (conjugate root theorem).
For a monic quartic, the product of the four roots equals the constant term \(E\) (sign \((-1)^4=+1\)).

keyPoints.note: Real coefficients ⇒ 3 − i and 1 + 2i are roots too; E is the product of all four roots.

questions.stem:
\(P(z)=z^4-10z^3+117z^2-412z+1460\).
\(P(z)\) has zeroes \(2a+bi\) and \(3a+2bi\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are integers.

parts.stem: Find the values of \(a\) and \(b\) and hence find all the zeroes of \(P(z)\).
parts.hint: Use the sum of zeroes for a, then the product of zeroes for b.

steps.explain: Real coefficients, so the conjugates are zeroes too.
Sum of the zeroes \(=-\frac ba=10\). The imaginary parts cancel.
Product of the zeroes \(=\frac ea=1460\). Multiply conjugate pairs: \((p+qi)(p-qi)=p^2+q^2\).
\(b\) is an integer, so \(b^2=16\), \(b=\pm4\). The zeroes are \(2\pm4i\) and \(3\pm8i\).

keyPoints.note: Include the conjugates. Sum of zeroes gives a; product of zeroes gives a quadratic in b².

parts.stem: Factorise \(P(z)\) into its quadratic factors with real coefficients.
parts.hint: Each conjugate pair p ± qi gives z² − 2pz + (p² + q²).

steps.explain: A conjugate pair \(p\pm qi\) gives the factor \(z^2-(\text{sum})z+(\text{product})=z^2-2pz+(p^2+q^2)\).

keyPoints.note: Pair each zero with its conjugate: z² − (sum)z + (product).

parts.stem: Explain why \(z^4=(z-1)^4\) does not have four roots.

steps.explain: Move everything to one side and expand.
The \(z^4\) terms cancel, leaving a polynomial of degree 3. A degree-3 polynomial has at most 3 roots.

options: Because the equation only has real roots.
Expanding, \(z^4-(z-1)^4\) is a cubic (the \(z^4\) terms cancel), so it has at most 3 roots.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: z⁴ − (z − 1)⁴ — what is its degree?

parts.hint: Let x = z/(z − 1) so x⁴ = 1; solve each case for z.

steps.explain: \(z=1\) is not a solution, so divide by \((z-1)^4\) and let \(x=\frac{z}{z-1}\).
The cubic has real coefficients, so the conjugate is also a root (it comes from \(x=-i\)).

keyPoints.note: Divide by (z − 1)⁴: (z/(z − 1))⁴ = 1, so z/(z − 1) is a fourth root of unity.

questions.stem: For which positive integers n is \((1+i\sqrt3)^n\) purely imaginary?
questions.hint: Its argument is \(n\pi/3\). A nonzero purely imaginary number has argument \(\pi/2+k\pi\).

steps.work: The left side is even and the right side is odd, impossible for integer k.

keyPoints.note: Its argument is \(n\pi/3\). A nonzero purely imaginary number has argument \(\pi/2+k\pi\).

Check: \(2\left(\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}+i\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)=2\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac12i\right)=-\sqrt3+i\) ✓. A calculator \(\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1}{-\sqrt3}\right)=-\frac\pi6\) gives the wrong quadrant.

keyPoints.note: |w| = 2; w is in the 2nd quadrant, so arg w = π − π/6.

parts.hint: Use de Moivre's theorem on w = 2 cis(5π/6), then reduce the argument.

steps.explain: Use the result of part (i) and de Moivre's theorem \((r\operatorname{cis}\theta)^n=r^n\operatorname{cis}n\theta\).
Bring the argument into \((-\pi,\pi]\) by subtracting a multiple of \(2\pi\).
A shorter route: factor out \(w\) and use \(w^6\).

parts.answer: Using \(w=2\operatorname{cis}\frac{5\pi}{6}\) and de Moivre's theorem: \(w^7=2^7\operatorname{cis}\frac{35\pi}{6}=128\operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{35\pi}{6}-6\pi\right)=128\operatorname{cis}\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=128\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-\frac12i\right)=64\sqrt3-64i\). Also \(64w=-64\sqrt3+64i\). Adding, \(w^7+64w=0\). (Alternatively \(w^6=64\operatorname{cis}5\pi=-64\), so \(w^7+64w=w(w^6+64)=0\).)

keyPoints.note: Apply de Moivre to 2 cis(5π/6); 35π/6 − 6π = −π/6.

questions.stem:
The argument of a complex number \(z\) is \(\frac{\pi}{7}\).
What is \(\operatorname{Arg}\left(z^{10}\right)\) equal to?
questions.hint: Multiply the argument by 10, then bring it into (−π, π] by subtracting 2π.

steps.explain: By de Moivre's theorem, raising to the 10th power multiplies the argument by 10.
\(\operatorname{Arg}\) (capital A) means the principal argument, which must lie in \((-\pi,\pi]\). \(\frac{10\pi}{7}\gt\pi\), so subtract \(2\pi\).
So \(\operatorname{Arg}(z^{10})=\frac{-4\pi}{7}\), option D. (\(\frac{3\pi}{7}\) comes from subtracting only \(\pi\).)

keyPoints.note: Capital-A Arg is the principal argument: it must be in (−π, π].

questions.stem: For \(z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\), prove \(z^n-\frac1{z^n}=2i\sin n\theta\).
questions.hint: Use De Moivre’s theorem and the fact that |z|=1, so the reciprocal reverses the sign of the imaginary part.
questions.solution: Sample answer: By De Moivre, zⁿ=cos(nθ)+i sin(nθ). Since |z|=1, z⁻ⁿ=cos(nθ)−i sin(nθ). Subtracting gives 2i sin(nθ).

steps.explain: Apply De Moivre’s theorem to the nth power.
Since z lies on the unit circle, its reciprocal has the opposite argument.

questions.answer: Sample answer: By De Moivre, zⁿ=cos(nθ)+i sin(nθ). Since |z|=1, z⁻ⁿ=cos(nθ)−i sin(nθ). Subtracting gives 2i sin(nθ).

keyPoints.note: Recognise that z has modulus 1 and use De Moivre’s theorem.

parts.hint: Solve for 4θ in [0, 4π] first, using tan's period π, then divide by 4.

steps.explain: If \(0\le\theta\le\pi\) then \(0\le4\theta\le4\pi\), so look for all solutions of \(\tan(4\theta)=1\) in that range.
The basic angle is \(\frac\pi4\), and \(\tan\) repeats every \(\pi\).

keyPoints.note: Find every 4θ in [0, 4π] with tan = 1 (period π), then divide by 4.

parts.hint: Put A = B = θ in tan(A + B).

steps.explain: Use the compound angle formula with \(A=B=\theta\).

keyPoints.note: Use tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B) with A = B = θ.

parts.hint: Apply the tan 2θ formula to 4θ = 2(2θ), then clear the fractions.

steps.explain: Apply the double-angle formula to \(4\theta=2(2\theta)\). Write \(t=\tan\theta\).

keyPoints.note: Use tan 4θ = 2 tan 2θ / (1 − tan²2θ) and substitute tan 2θ = 2t/(1 − t²).

parts.hint: Put x = tan θ in (iii) with tan 4θ = 1, then use the solutions from (i).

steps.explain: Multiply out and collect all terms on one side.
So every \(\theta\) with \(\tan4\theta=1\) gives a root \(x=\tan\theta\). From (i) there are four such \(\theta\) in \([0,\pi]\).
These four tangents are all different (two are positive, from the first quadrant; two are negative, from the second), and a quartic has at most four roots. So they are exactly the roots.

parts.answer: Let \(x=\tan\theta\) where \(\tan4\theta=1\). By (iii), \(\frac{4x-4x^3}{1-6x^2+x^4}=1\), so \(1-6x^2+x^4=4x-4x^3\), i.e. \(x^4+4x^3-6x^2-4x+1=0\). By (i) the solutions of \(\tan4\theta=1\) in \([0,\pi]\) are \(\theta=\frac\pi{16},\frac{5\pi}{16},\frac{9\pi}{16},\frac{13\pi}{16}\); their tangents are four different numbers, so they are the four roots of the quartic.

keyPoints.note: Set x = tan θ and tan 4θ = 1 in (iii); the θ values from (i) give the four roots.

parts.hint: Product of the roots of a quartic is e/a.

steps.explain: The four numbers are the roots of \(x^4+4x^3-6x^2-4x+1=0\) from (iv).
For a quartic \(ax^4+bx^3+cx^2+dx+e=0\), the product of the roots is \(+\frac ea\).
Check with complementary angles: \(\tan\frac{9\pi}{16}=-\cot\frac{\pi}{16}\) and \(\tan\frac{13\pi}{16}=-\cot\frac{5\pi}{16}\), so the product is \((-1)(-1)\cdot1\cdot1=1\).

keyPoints.note: These are the roots of the quartic in (iv); for a quartic the product of roots is e/a.

parts.stem:
Reduce the quartic equation in (iv) to a quadratic equation in terms of \(u\) where \(u=x-\frac{1}{x}\) to then show:

\(\tan\frac{\pi}{16}-\cot\frac{\pi}{16}=-2-2\sqrt2.\)
parts.hint: Divide by x², use x² + 1/x² = u² + 2, then decide the sign of u for x = tan(π/16).

steps.explain: Divide the quartic by \(x^2\) (\(x\neq0\), since 0 is not a root).

Choose the right root for \(x=\tan\frac\pi{16}\). Since \(0 \lt \frac\pi{16} \lt \frac\pi4\), we have \(0 \lt x \lt 1\), so \(\frac1x \gt 1 \gt x\) and \(u=x-\frac1x \lt 0\). Of the two roots, \(-2+2\sqrt2\approx0.83\) is positive, so
Numerical check: \(\tan\frac\pi{16}\approx0.1989\) and \(\cot\frac\pi{16}\approx5.0273\); the difference is \(\approx-4.828=-2-2\sqrt2\) ✓.

parts.answer: Divide the quartic by \(x^2\ (\neq0)\): \(x^2+\frac1{x^2}+4\left(x-\frac1x\right)-6=0\). Since \(x^2+\frac1{x^2}=u^2+2\), this is \(u^2+4u-4=0\), so \(u=-2\pm2\sqrt2\). For \(x=\tan\frac\pi{16}\), \(0 \lt x \lt 1\) so \(u=x-\frac1x \lt 0\); the only negative root is \(-2-2\sqrt2\). Hence \(\tan\frac\pi{16}-\cot\frac\pi{16}=-2-2\sqrt2\).

keyPoints.note: Divide by x² and use x² + 1/x² = (x − 1/x)² + 2 to get u² + 4u − 4 = 0.

questions.stem: The roots of \(z^n=1\) form a regular n-gon on the unit circle. Prove its perimeter is \(P_n=2n\sin(\pi/n)\).
questions.hint: Adjacent roots subtend a central angle of 2π/n; use the isosceles triangle chord length.
questions.solution: Sample answer: Consecutive nth roots lie on the unit circle and subtend angle 2π/n. Bisecting the isosceles triangle formed with the origin gives half a side sin(π/n), so each side is 2sin(π/n). There are n sides, hence P_n=2n sin(π/n).

steps.explain: Find the angle between adjacent roots.

steps.work: Each half has hypotenuse 1 and angle \(\pi/n\), so half a side is \(\sin(\pi/n)\).

steps.explain: Find one side and multiply by n.

questions.stem: The exact value of \(e^{\left(\frac{i\pi}{8}\right)}\) is:
questions.hint: Raise e^(iπ/8) to the 4th power and see which number you get.

steps.explain: Raise \(e^{i\pi/8}\) to the fourth power using index laws.
So \(e^{i\pi/8}\) is a fourth root of \(i\). It is the principal fourth root, because its argument \(\frac\pi8\) is the argument of \(i\) divided by 4.

questions.stem: If \((x+iy)^6=e^{2i\pi}\), where \(x,y\) are real, find a non-zero solution for \(x\) and \(y\).
questions.hint: e^(2iπ) = 1, so x + iy is a sixth root of unity: cis(kπ/3).

steps.explain: So \(x+iy\) is a sixth root of unity: modulus 1 and argument a multiple of \(\frac{2\pi}{6}=\frac{\pi}{3}\).

questions.stem: Find the four 4th roots of \(-1\) and show them on an Argand diagram.
questions.hint: z⁴ = cis π: the first root has argument π/4, then add π/2 each time.

steps.explain: Write \(-1\) in modulus–argument form and let \(z=\operatorname{cis}\theta\) (all roots have modulus 1).
On the Argand diagram they are equally spaced (\(\frac{\pi}{2}\) apart) on the unit circle, one in each quadrant: \(\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2}i\).

questions.stem: Let \(\omega\) be a complex cube root of unity. Prove that if \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) then \(1+\omega^n+\omega^{2n}=3\) if \(n\) is a multiple of 3 or 0 if \(n\) is not a multiple of 3.
questions.hint: Use ω³ = 1 and 1 + ω + ω² = 0; split into n = 3X, 3X + 1, 3X + 2.

steps.explain: \(\omega\) is a complex (non-real) cube root of unity, so \(\omega^3=1\) and \(\omega\neq1\). Factorise \(\omega^3-1\).
Every natural number is of one of these three forms, so the result is proved.

questions.answer: \(\omega^3=1\), \(\omega\neq1\), so \(\omega^2+\omega+1=0\) (from \(\omega^3-1=(\omega-1)(\omega^2+\omega+1)\)). If n = 3X: \(1+(\omega^3)^X+(\omega^3)^{2X}=1+1+1=3\). If n = 3X + 1: \(1+\omega^{3X}\omega+\omega^{6X}\omega^2=1+\omega+\omega^2=0\). If n = 3X + 2: \(1+\omega^{3X}\omega^2+\omega^{6X}\omega^4=1+\omega^2+\omega=0\) (since \(\omega^4=\omega\)).

keyPoints.note: ω³ = 1 and ω ≠ 1 give 1 + ω + ω² = 0. Consider the remainder of n on division by 3.

questions.stem:
Let \(z\) be a complex number such that \(z^3=\frac{i}{\overline{z}}\).
Which of the following is a possible value for \(z\)?
questions.hint: Multiply by z̄ and use z = re^(iθ): you get r⁴e^(2iθ) = i.

steps.explain: So \(z=e^{i\pi/4}\) (or \(e^{-3i\pi/4}\)). Check A: \(z^3\overline z=e^{3i\pi/4}e^{-i\pi/4}=e^{i\pi/2}=i\) ✓. The others give \(-i\), \(e^{2i\pi/3}\), \(e^{-2i\pi/3}\).

keyPoints.note: Multiply by z̄: z³z̄ = r⁴e^(2iθ). Compare with i = e^(iπ/2).
